One imagines a fellow of some influence; a man with a particular desire to gratify.” He turned the book over in his hands, his smile conveying a knowledge he did not quite possess, but which he was determined to pretend to. Eleanor Morton said nothing, her attention fixed upon a loose thread on her glove, which she seemed intent on worrying into a state of complete ruin.

“And the dedication,” he continued, opening to the frontispiece, “‘For H., whose constancy is the only sun I seek.’ Very affecting, is it not? I wonder who this ‘H.’ might be. A Helen? A Harriet? Such a public yet private declaration must be a source of great pleasure, or perhaps great anxiety.” He looked directly at her. She felt the gaze, for a faint colour rose in her cheek, but she would not meet it.

“I believe, sir,” she said, her voice admirably steady, “that poets often employ initials for mere effect, without a particular object in view.”

“For effect! Aye, that is one explanation. Another is that there is a very particular object, but one whose name cannot be written in full. I confess, I prefer the latter. It is so much more romantic. What do you say, Miss Bennet? Am I too romantic in my interpretations?”

Catherine Bennet, who had been observing this exchange with an enjoyment she knew to be unkind, felt obliged to answer. “I should think, Mr. Alistair, that you find the interpretation that provides the most entertainment.”

“Precisely! You understand me perfectly. There is no pleasure in a simple story. Now, this poet, this ‘Lover of Truth’ as he styles himself; I cannot conjecture who he might be. Perhaps a gentleman we know?” He paused, and in the silence, Eleanor’s needle, which she had taken up, slipped and pricked her finger. I have the honour, madam, (to Mrs. Dale, the lady of the house,) of having unsettled your entire party with a simple book of poems.”

“I think you bold,” she whispered back. “She must guess your meaning.”

“And you are to be the instrument of her shame?”

“I am to be the instrument of truth, which is a much grander thing. Look; she has turned a page. ‘Ode to a Distant Star.’ How very fitting. I believe that is his most famous one.”

What is the point of a poem if it does not jingle at the end? Tell me that.” The listeners were much diverted by this, and even Eleanor could not suppress a small, genuine smile. Mr. Green says he is quite the celebrity in certain circles.”

So the ‘H.’ of the dedication was for himself all along! How wonderfully vain. Is it not so, Miss Morton? To dedicate a work to oneself?”

Eleanor looked up, and for the first time, her eyes met his directly. A calm dignity had settled on her features, replacing the earlier anxiety. “On the contrary, sir,” she said, her voice clear and cool. “I should think a man who has laboured in obscurity might be forgiven for claiming his own heart as his first and most faithful admirer. The reflection that looked back at her was of a stranger; a young woman whose customary sparkle was extinguished, whose eyes were shadowed with a misery she had never before known.

The tenderness in his gaze as he looked at her. That look—that was the heart of the matter. Emma had seen Mr. Knightley look at many people in many ways; with approbation, with irritation, with amusement, with brotherly affection for herself. But she had never seen that look before. It was a look of profound, quiet, and settled regard; it was the look of a man who has found his object, and is content.

Mr. Knightley, her friend, her guide, her critic, the one constant and unimpeachable presence in her life, had been quietly, steadily, falling in love. Had she not been the one to insist upon Jane’s merits, to force them together on social occasions, to create the very opportunities for this attachment to form? The irony was so bitter, it was almost a physical pain.

The world outside was still and silent, as insensible to her turmoil as her father had been. A misery so profound settled upon her that it felt like a permanent alteration of her being. It was not the sharp, indignant sting of a wounded vanity, such as she had felt after Mr. Elton’s proposal. This was a deeper, hollower ache. It was loss. The prospect no longer terrified her. It was, she thought, exactly as it should be.

She confessed her suspicions, the theory she had developed with Frank Churchill, and the way they had teased the subject in Jane’s very presence. “I see it now for what it was,” she concluded miserably. “A piece of thoughtless, unfeeling persecution. And Mr. Knightley saw it all. No wonder he is angry with me. He was right. He is always right.”

The admission cost her a great deal, and she felt a tear escape and trace a cold path down her cheek. Mrs. Weston squeezed her hand. “It is a sign of your good heart, Emma, that you feel this now. You were mistaken, perhaps. We all are, from time to time. But your desire to amuse yourself ran away with your better judgment. It does not make you a cruel person. As for Jane Fairfax, she is a very reserved young woman. It is difficult to know what she is feeling. But I am sure she has borne no lasting resentment.”

“I do not know how you can say so. I saw the blush on her face. She was in agony, and we were amusing ourselves with it. He was amusing himself with it. I begin to think, Mrs. Weston,” said Emma, her voice full of a new and startling conviction, “that I do not like Mr. Frank Churchill very much at all.”

Before Mrs. Weston could reply to this extraordinary declaration, their conversation was interrupted by the appearance of Mr. Weston himself, who came bustling down the path from the house, a letter in his hand.

“News!” he cried, waving the letter triumphantly. “News from town! A letter from Frank. He sends his best to you, Emma. Says he is counting the days until you are all in London together.” He beamed at them both, the very picture of a happy and unsuspecting father.

“What does he say, my love?” asked Mrs. Weston, her attention diverted at once to her stepson.

“Oh, the usual,” said Mr. Weston, scanning the page. “Full of nonsense. He has seen a new play, which he declares is detestable, though he seems to have sat through it twice. He has bought a new horse, which he fears is a little lame, but was such a bargain he could not resist it. And he has had his hair cut. A complete success, he says. By a man named Edwards, in some street I have never heard of. He says he is a new man.” Mr. Weston chuckled. “And, what is this?” He peered at the letter more closely. “Ah! He says he called at Brunswick Square. Found them all at home. John Knightley was deep in some legal papers, and Isabella was worrying about one of the children’s coughs. And Mr. Knightley, it seems, was preparing to leave London.”

“Leave London!” exclaimed Emma and Mrs. Weston in a single breath.

“So it says,” confirmed Mr. Weston, tapping the letter. “‘Knightley is returning to Surrey,’ he writes. ‘He talks of business at Donwell that cannot be postponed. I believe he finds London society little to his taste at present, or perhaps it is only the society at his brother’s that he wishes to escape. John can be a very dull dog when he is busy.’ Frank is too hard on John Knightley,” Mr. Weston commented, folding the letter. “A more upright, honourable man does not exist. But there you have it. Knightley is returning to Donwell. He will probably be home before the week is out.”

Emma sat in stunned silence. The entire landscape of her misery had been altered in a single moment. He was not staying in London to rebuke her. He was coming back. He was running away from London, just as she had planned to run away from Highbury. The reversal was so complete, so bewildering, that she could not immediately grasp its meaning.

“Well!” said Mrs. Weston, breaking the silence. “That is settled, then. You see, Emma? It was just a brief visit. Business, as I said.” She gave Emma’s hand a final, reassuring pat.

But Emma was scarcely listening. A wild, tumultuous hope was rising in her breast. He was coming back. The awkward meeting in London, the trial before the tribunal of her family, would not take place. She would not have to face his displeasure under his brother’s roof. He was returning to Highbury. To Donwell. To her world.

And she was still going to London.

The irony was so profound, so exquisite, it was almost comical. He had fled Highbury to avoid her, and she had planned to flee to London to avoid him. Now, by a strange and unexpected manoeuvre of fate, they had merely exchanged positions. He was returning to the very place she was leaving. They were like two figures in a country dance, moving in opposite directions, always missing each other.

A slow smile spread across Emma’s face, a genuine smile, the first in a fortnight. “So,” she said, her voice light and airy once more. “I shall go to London after all.”

Mr. Weston beamed. “Of course you will! And you will have a capital time. And now you must both come in and take some refreshment. I have had a new cask of sherry laid down, and I should like your opinion of it.”

As she walked towards the house between her two kind friends, Emma felt as if a great weight had been lifted from her. The future, which had seemed so fraught with difficulty, was suddenly full of possibility again. Mr. Knightley was coming home. She did not know what it meant, or what would happen when she returned from London herself. But for now, it was enough. It was more than enough. He was coming home, and she, for the first time in what felt like an age, was truly happy to be leaving it. The trip to London was no longer an escape or a trial; it was simply a visit to her sister. And when she came back, he would be there. Whatever had been broken between them would have to be mended, not in the cold, formal drawing-room of Brunswick Square, but here, in Highbury, on their own ground. The prospect no longer terrified her. It was, she thought, exactly as it should be.
